1.title: Change, Improvement, Culture and the External Environment
1.text: Welcome to Module 12, the last Business Environment module. Four kinds of change meet here. Changes to the project, which is change control. Changes to how we work, which is continuous improvement. Changes to the organization and its culture. And changes in the world outside the project. In Part 1, we cover change control. Part 2 covers lessons learned, improvement and culture. Part 3 covers organizational change and the external environment.

1.title: Where This Module Sits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits. The Business Environment domain has eight tasks, and this module covers four. Task three: manage and control changes. Task six: continuous improvement. Task seven: support organizational change. Task eight: evaluate external business environment changes. A habit that helps on the exam: work out which kind of change a scenario describes. A change to the project goes through change control. A change to the way of working goes through improvement. A change to the organization needs people support. A change outside needs scanning and assessment.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Run the change control process and know who decides. Implement approved changes and update every document. Use lessons learned and continuous improvement properly. Assess culture and support the organization through change. Survey and assess external changes and respond through the right channel. And tell change control, change management and improvement apart.

1.title: Case Check-In: A Change Request
1.text: Here is a change on our microgrid. The Cryo-Imaging Lab asks for a larger battery reserve, to protect sensitive equipment during outages. You log it. You assess the impact on cost, schedule, risk, benefits and compliance. And you take it to the change board, because it exceeds your threshold. Meanwhile, keep executing planned work and keep analyzing impact and risk. If approved, implement it, and update the designs, baselines and backlog. Tell the lab the decision and the reason, whatever it is.

1.title: Change Control: Key Terms
1.text: Key terms. A change request is a formal proposal to modify a document, deliverable or baseline. Change control identifies, documents and approves or rejects changes. Integrated change control evaluates the impact across the whole project and then decides. A change control board is a formally chartered group, also called a steering committee, that approves, defers or rejects changes. The change management plan sets up the board, its authority and the change control system. The configuration management plan says which artifacts are controlled. And the change log lists submitted changes with their status.

1.title: Four Types of Change Request
1.text: Four types of change request. Corrective action brings performance back in line with the plan. Preventive action avoids a future problem. Defect repair fixes a nonconformance. An update modifies or adds to approved content. Any stakeholder may request a change, and it may be internal or external. Each request is approved, deferred or rejected. Do not confuse a change request with an issue or a risk. A change request modifies a baseline or document. An issue is a current problem. A risk is uncertainty. A change may be raised to address either.

1.title: Assess and Implement Changes
1.text: The Assess and Implement Changes process manages changes to scope, product scope, plan components and documents, so the project stays aligned with its objectives and constraints. Inputs include the change and configuration management plans, the baselines, the change log, the traceability matrix, the risk report and the change requests. Tools include expert judgment, change control tools, cost-benefit and multicriteria analysis, voting, and backlog management. Outputs are approved change requests, and updates to plans and documents. How formal it is depends on the project's scope, complexity, contract and approach.

1.title: Predictive Change Control
1.text: In predictive work, scope is not formally controlled until baselines exist. Once a baseline is approved, all changes go through the formal process. Requests may start verbally, but they must be documented in writing and entered in the change system. They typically include estimated schedule and cost impacts before approval. Each is approved, deferred or rejected by a designated person, such as the sponsor or project manager, or by the board. While awaiting the decision, keep executing planned work, and keep analyzing the impact and risks. After board approval, the customer or sponsor may need to approve, unless they sit on the board.

1.title: The Change Control Flow
1.text: The flow has seven steps. One, receive and log the request in writing, with an identifier, requester, date and status. Two, assess the impact across all domains, estimating effects on schedule and cost, and checking the business case and compliance. Three, develop options and recommend: implement, modify, defer or reject. Four, decide at the right level, recording the rationale. Five, communicate the decision. Six, implement through Manage Project Execution. Seven, verify that the change achieved its purpose, and close it in the log.

1.title: Impact Assessment
1.text: Assess the impact of a change across the whole project. Scope and requirements. Schedule and cost, with new estimates. Quality. Resources. Risk, including new risks and reserve use. Stakeholders. The business case and benefits. And compliance. A change that threatens the business case or external commitments needs the sponsor or governance, so that value is revalidated. Changes ripple, so a change to scope also changes cost, schedule, risk and often contracts.

1.title: Who Decides
1.text: Decide at the right level. The project manager decides within tolerance and authority. The change control board decides beyond that. The sponsor or customer decides above thresholds, and may need to confirm after the board. Governance decides when the business case is threatened. Know the thresholds in the change management plan or the governance framework. If none is defined for a decision above your authority, define it with the sponsor. Do not infer it from past decisions.

1.title: Governing Principles
1.text: Some governing principles. Never implement an unapproved change. Even a free improvement, a harmless deviation such as a higher-capacity part, or a verified fix is a change: assess its impact and submit it through change control. If it was already made, submit it retroactively and decide. Corrections of baseline errors, such as a wrong unit or a missed dependency, also go through change control. Scope creep and gold plating are uncontrolled changes. Do not freeze progress while a decision is pending. Emergency changes need a fast, authorized path and prompt documentation. And verify the results of an implemented change, and record the lessons.

1.title: Communicate the Status of Proposed Changes
1.text: Communicate the status of proposed changes. Keep the change log current, with a status for every request. Tell the requester the decision and the rationale, including for deferred and rejected requests. PMBOK 8 requires that. Inform affected stakeholders and the team of what changed and what it means for them: scope, dates, cost and roles. Report pending and approved changes in status reports and dashboards. Give board members clear packages with the description, impact analysis, options, recommendation and risks. In adaptive work, show the backlog and its order openly.

1.title: Implement Approved Changes
1.text: Approved changes are implemented through Manage Project Execution. Update the plan components and baselines, and funding requirements if needed, re-baselining only through the approved change. Adjust resources, procurement and contracts, with amendments or variation orders and new estimates. Update the risk register. Brief the team and stakeholders, and train if the way of working changes. Implement and test, and confirm that acceptance criteria still hold. Then monitor the effect: did the change deliver the benefit? And record lessons.

1.title: Update the Documents
1.text: An approval is not finished until the documents reflect it. Update baselines and plans: the scope, schedule and cost baselines and related management plans. Update requirements and design: the traceability matrix, specifications, drawings, backlog and acceptance criteria. Update registers and logs: the change log, risk register, assumption log, issue log, stakeholder register and lessons register. Update the schedule and cost records. Update contracts. And update configuration records. Keep one authoritative version in a controlled repository, with the same change reflected everywhere.

1.title: Configuration Management
1.text: Configuration management and change control are related. Configuration management identifies configuration items, records and reports their status, and verifies and audits versions, so the product stays consistent and accountability is kept. Change control identifies and documents changes, and approves, defers or rejects them, for documents, deliverables and baselines. Tools support both: they register requests, track assessment and approval, and manage the board's requests and decisions. Choose tools by stakeholder needs and organizational constraints, manual or automated.

1.title: Change in Adaptive Work
1.text: In adaptive work, change is managed mainly through backlog management, not formal change requests. A proposed change is recorded as a backlog item, and an impact analysis, lighter but not absent, evaluates its effect and priority. There is typically no formal approval: any proposed change can be added. A lower priority means the change is effectively deferred, and not adding it means it is rejected. The product owner orders the backlog by value. Formal approval applies only above contract or governance thresholds, such as a scope change above ten percent of effort.

1.title: Protecting the Iteration
1.text: Protect the iteration. New requests from executives go to the backlog through the product owner, and the project manager represents the team's capacity and shows the trade-offs. Update the roadmap and backlog regularly, because customer feedback and market learning change them. Routine backlog changes flow normally, and those above a contractual threshold go through formal approval. In hybrid work, formal control covers the baselined envelope: milestones, committed scope, budget and regulatory commitments. The backlog adapts inside it. Impact analysis still happens in adaptive work. It is lighter, not absent.

1.title: Change Control by Approach
1.text: Change control looks different by approach. Predictive: a written change request, impact analysis with cost and schedule, a board or designated approver, and a baseline update. Agile: a backlog item, lighter impact analysis, the product owner ordering by value, and formal approval only above thresholds. Hybrid: formal control for the envelope of milestones, committed scope and budget, with the backlog adapting inside it, and a request only if the envelope moves. Name the mechanism that fits the approach in the scenario.

1.title: Change Control Traps: What PMI Expects
1.text: The traps for change control. No unapproved changes, even free, beneficial or tested ones. Assess impact first, then decide, document in writing, and log everything. Know the authority level, and define missing thresholds with the sponsor. Keep working while waiting for the decision, and communicate all outcomes, including deferred and rejected requests. Implement and update everything: schedule, drawings, backlog and documents. Baseline corrections are changes. Agile change goes through the backlog. And do not confuse the change management plan with organizational change management.

1.title: Part 1 Recap
1.text: Let us recap Part 1. There are four types of change request: corrective, preventive, defect repair and update. The flow is log, assess, recommend, decide, communicate, implement and verify. Decide at the right level, and define missing thresholds with the sponsor. Never implement an unapproved change, count baseline corrections as changes, and keep working while you wait. Update every document the change affects. And match the mechanism to the approach: formal requests, the backlog, or a formal envelope with a backlog inside. In Part 2, we look at lessons, improvement and culture.

2.title: Lessons Learned: Key Terms
2.text: Part 2 covers learning and improving. Key terms. The lessons learned register is a project document of knowledge gained, created early and updated throughout. The lessons learned repository is the organizational asset that receives it when a project or phase ends. A retrospective is a regular workshop to improve process and product, at least at the end of every iteration. An after-action review is a structured review of what happened and what to learn. An in-progress postmortem is a structured review at stages of the life cycle. And continuous improvement means incremental improvement of processes, products and services.

2.title: Where Lessons Come From
2.text: Lessons come from many places. Retrospectives, at least each iteration. After-action reviews, at the end of the project or after significant milestones. In-progress postmortems, periodically. Quality audits, which identify good practices and nonconformities. Issues, realized risks and opportunities, variances and trends. Stakeholder feedback and benchmarking against comparable organizations. And Close Project or Phase adds the final lessons. Capture lessons as events happen, while details are fresh. Waiting for one session at the end loses detail and delays use.

2.title: Lessons Across the Life of a Project
2.text: Use lessons at three moments. Before and in planning: search the repository before planning, and use lessons to shape the approach, estimates, risk checklists and reserves. While the work proceeds: capture as events happen, act quickly, and look for patterns, because the same issue in several entries is a systemic problem. At phase and project end: close the phase formally first, then capture its lessons and carry them into the next phase. Hold a final session for project-level lessons, even if retrospectives ran every iteration.

2.title: Using Lessons in Planning
2.text: Use lessons in planning. Approach and tailoring: what worked on similar projects. Estimates: analogous estimating uses actual durations and costs of earlier projects, adjusted for known differences. Risk identification: checklists built from completed projects list risks that occurred before. Reserves and buffers: base them on the specific causes an earlier project suffered, like late permits or commissioning problems, not on a generic pad. Templates and structures. And stakeholder, procurement and quality history. Search the repository before planning, and record which lessons you used.

2.title: What Makes Lessons Usable
2.text: Lessons are usable when they are specific and actionable, with a category, description, impact, recommendation and proposed action. They are searchable and accessible in a controlled repository, ideally with a way to contact the originators. They are analyzed for common issues that call for changes to procedures. And they are owned and checked: someone applies each lesson, and a later review confirms it changed something. Common failures: logging only at the end, a long unsearchable log, a generic buffer, no owner, and blame instead of learning.

2.title: Continuous Improvement in Practice
2.text: Continuous improvement means small, repeated improvements. Commit to a few improvements from each retrospective. Put them in the next iteration's backlog or plan, with an owner and a date. And check the result at the next review. A long action list or a log does not change anything. If the same format yields the same ideas, or results stop improving, inspect and adapt the improvement process itself. Change the format and bring data. Track follow-through, and rotate the facilitator. And add cross-team sessions. More of the same process gives more of the same results.

2.title: Shared Problems and Systemic Fixes
2.text: Shared problems need shared fixes. If several teams report the same issue, run a cross-team analysis and fix. Separate retrospectives lack the full picture. Look for patterns across entries, iterations and teams, and fix them at the system level, not team by team. Standardize best practices: where teams keep varying checklists or templates, consolidate them into one tested standard and update the asset. A proven procedure goes to the asset owner. And check the effect of an improvement before standardizing it.

2.title: Improvement Approaches
2.text: PMBOK 8 names several approaches. Plan-do-check-act is the basic loop of small repeated cycles. Lean maximizes value and eliminates waste, using value stream mapping. Total Quality Management is an organization-wide commitment to quality where everyone owns it. Six Sigma is data-driven reduction of defects and variation. The Five Focusing Steps from the theory of constraints identify the constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else to it, elevate it, and repeat. And Kaizen is continual small improvement. The exam asks which fits the situation.

2.title: Improvement at Four Levels
2.text: Improvement works at four levels. The team improves through retrospectives and a few committed actions. The project improves through lessons, audits and process analysis. The organization improves through updates to process assets, such as standard checklists and templates. And governance improves through feedback loops: periodic reviews, lessons learned and iterative adjustments. Teams own and improve their processes, while organizations provide methodologies as starting points. Review points, gates and retrospectives are chances to inspect and adapt.

2.title: Two Kinds of Process Asset
2.text: Organizational process assets come in two categories. Policies, processes and procedures are usually set by the PMO or another function outside the project. They are generally not updated as part of project work, but only through the organization's own update policy. The team may tailor templates, life cycles and checklists for its project. Knowledge repositories, in contrast, are updated throughout the project with project information. That includes lessons learned, financial performance and metrics. It includes issues and defects, completed schedules, risk data and earned value data.

2.title: Updating Organizational Assets
2.text: To update an organizational asset, follow six steps. Prove it: show results from a pilot or project data. Document it: draft the new version with the evidence and the reason. Submit it to the owner of the asset, the PMO or process owner. Review and approve it under the organization's update policy. Publish a new controlled version and retire the old one. Communicate, train if needed, and check adoption. Do not change the master copy on your own, or update before it is proven. Forward suggestions for policies to the appropriate unit.

2.title: Improvement in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
2.text: Improvement looks different by approach. Predictive: capture points at gates, reviews, postmortems, audits and closure, with plan updates through change control and process changes at gates. The risk is lessons collected too late. Agile: a retrospective each iteration and a release retrospective, with actions going into the next backlog and working agreements changing at once. The risk is retrospectives that change nothing. Hybrid: the envelope through change control while team practices adapt. Do not skip short retrospectives because things went well or work is heavy.

2.title: Improvement Traps: What PMI Expects
2.text: The traps for improvement. Capture lessons throughout, not only at the end. Use lessons to shape the plan: specific lessons beat a generic buffer. Make lessons accessible and walk the next team through them. Retrospective actions must be implemented, and when the process stagnates, update the improvement process itself. Shared problems need a cross-team fix, and best practices are standardized in the assets. Policies owned elsewhere change only through the organization's policy. Do not blame, because a blame culture stops sharing. And a cancelled project still closes formally.

2.title: The Project as a Vehicle of Change
2.text: Now the organization. A project moves the organization from its current state, perhaps through a transition state, to a future state. Success means the organization reaches the future state and gets the value key stakeholders defined. Delivery is not value: value appears when people use what was delivered. That is why PMBOK 8 asks for transition and readiness requirements, such as training and data conversion, and a plan to maintain value. There are two sides to manage: the product side, and the people side.

2.title: Change Control Versus Change Management
2.text: Do not confuse two kinds of change. Change control, with the board, baselines and change requests, governs changes to the project. Change management moves the organization's people to the future state: readiness, engagement, training and support. PMBOK 8 defines change management as a comprehensive, cyclic, structured approach for transitioning individuals, groups and organizations to a future state. It is not change control, and not the Guide's change management plan. Baseline changes caused by organizational change still go through change control.

2.title: Assess Organizational Culture
2.text: Assess organizational culture. Structure: fixed, hierarchical structures lean predictive, and network-oriented ones suit adaptive or hybrid. Management style: a culture of managing and directing fits predictive, while one that embraces uncertainty fits adaptive. Risk attitude: risk-averse cultures prefer detailed, fixed schedules. Communication: flat organizations use open, informal channels, hierarchical ones use formal approaches. Decision-making, buy-in and trust, maturity, ethics, and attitude to change complete the picture. Review the environmental factors, interview and survey, and use cultural intelligence without stereotyping.

2.title: When Way of Working and Culture Do Not Match
2.text: When the way of working and the culture do not match, coach and tailor. Take an agile pilot in a hierarchical organization, where managers expect detailed plans and signed weekly reports. It needs coaching for the managers, and tailored reporting, such as milestones with iteration plans beneath. Use a hybrid where one part of the culture requires baselines and another benefits from iteration. Pilot the new practice, show results, then widen it. Do not force an approach on a culture that cannot support it, and do not abandon it at the first friction.

2.title: When the Organization Changes
2.text: Now organizational change: a merger, restructuring, a new sponsor or a shift in strategy. Follow five steps. Confirm the facts with the sponsor and governance: what is changing, when, and what is unknown. Assess the impact across the project. Determine the actions: continue as planned, adapt within your authority, raise a change request, escalate, or recommend pausing or stopping through governance. Act and communicate. And monitor and reassess. Do not pause everything, do not continue unchanged, and do not decide alone.

2.title: Impact Areas
2.text: Assess the impact across the project. Objectives and business case: do the objectives, success criteria and benefits still hold? Scope and requirements: what changes in needs and backlog? Schedule and budget: new dates, funding and approvals? Resources and team: who is reassigned, lost or added? Stakeholders and sponsor: new decision-makers and expectations. Governance and authority: new approval paths and thresholds. Contracts and risks: new terms, risks and obligations. The value proposition is the primary factor in deciding whether to continue, replan or end.

2.title: Typical Actions for Organizational Change
2.text: Match the action to the change. A new sponsor or key stakeholder: brief them, and reconfirm objectives, success criteria and support. Team members reassigned: plan the transition with the new leaders, hand over knowledge, and update the resource plan through change control. Strategy or priorities shift: revalidate the business case, and recommend continue, adapt or stop. Funding or headcount cut: reprioritize scope with the sponsor and use change control. A merger that changes platforms or vendors: evaluate the impact with the sponsor, and replan.

2.title: Part 2 Recap
2.text: Let us recap Part 2. Capture lessons throughout the project, use them before planning, and make them usable. Improvement means a few committed actions, with the results checked, and the improvement process itself adapted when it stalls. Tailor policies, and update repositories through their owners. Change control moves the project, while change management moves people. Assess culture first, then coach, pilot or use a hybrid. And when the organization changes, evaluate the impact with the sponsor, then act. In Part 3, we support people through change, and survey the external environment.

3.title: Case Check-In: Organizational Change
3.text: Part 3 begins with the microgrid. Suppose a new Provost arrives and Campus Facilities is restructured. Brief the new Provost and reconfirm objectives, success criteria and support, and update the stakeholder register. Plan the transition with the new Facilities leaders, hand over knowledge, and update the resource plan. The Cryo-Imaging Lab remains resistant: involve the lab in shaping the cut-over plan and connect the purpose to outcomes they value. And plan adoption: Facilities staff trained by doing, with adoption measured after handover.

3.title: Supporting People Through Change
3.text: Plan the people side into the project. Assess readiness: who is affected, how, and how prepared they are. Explain the why, in terms each group values, using two-way channels. Involve people in designing the new way. Plan specific change activities in the schedule and budget: communications, training, coaching, pilots and support channels. Make sponsorship visible. Hand adoption to the business owner after closure. Reinforce: celebrate quick wins, keep support available after go-live, and measure adoption and benefits, not only delivery.

3.title: Managing Resistance
3.text: Find the cause of resistance, then match the action. Fear of losing control or role: involve people in shaping new roles and decisions. No visible benefit: connect the purpose to outcomes they value, and share evidence. Habit: pilots, side-by-side use and simpler steps. Lack of skill: training, practice and coaching. Change fatigue: sequence changes, show quick wins, check capacity. Distrust from past changes: listen, keep small commitments, be transparent. Typical wrong answers: mandating use, training on features only, arguing the strategic case, and escalating to force compliance.

3.title: Change Models
3.text: As exam practice, you may meet several models. Lewin: unfreeze, change, refreeze. Kotter's eight steps: create urgency, build a guiding coalition, and form a vision. Enlist volunteers and remove barriers. Generate short-term wins, sustain momentum, and anchor the change in the culture. ADKAR: awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement. Bridges: endings, the neutral zone and new beginnings. The change curve: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. The exam asks for the best action. Spotting the gap matters more than naming the model.

3.title: Organizational Change in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
3.text: Organizational change looks different by approach. Predictive: a formal impact assessment, a change request and re-baseline, a communication plan, training before go-live and readiness gates. Resistance may be discovered late. Agile: the backlog is reprioritized with the product owner, and the team agreement is revisited when members change. Frequent demos involve users early, and incremental release allows phased adoption. The risk is team reshuffles and change fatigue. Team agreements are co-created with the whole team, including newcomers.

3.title: The External Environment
3.text: Environmental factors are conditions not under the team's immediate control that influence, constrain or direct the project. The internal environment sits inside the larger external environment. External groups include marketplace conditions, social and cultural influences, and legal restrictions. They include government and industry standards, and public health and safety regulations. They include financial considerations, physical environmental elements, emerging technologies and academic research. Their effect can be favorable, unfavorable or neutral. The Standard also stresses global pressures such as climate change, resource constraints and geopolitical instability.

3.title: Survey Changes to the External Environment
3.text: The ECO names four families to survey. Regulations: laws, rules, standards and enforcement. Technology: platforms, tools, competitors' technology and AI. Geopolitical conditions: sanctions, trade rules and instability. And markets: competitors, demand, prices and customer behavior. Financial, social, public health and climate factors belong here too. Prompt lists help. PESTLE covers political, economic, sociocultural, technological, legal and environmental. TECOP covers technical, environmental, commercial, operational and political. VUCA covers volatility, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity.

3.title: A Routine Scan
3.text: Make scanning routine. Name owners and sources: regulators and legal counsel, standards bodies, trade press, customers, suppliers, the PMO and compliance teams. Add an external scan to backlog refinement, planning, reviews, gates and steering meetings, not just kickoff. Record findings in the risk register, assumption log, stakeholder register and backlog. Sort the signals: confirmed or proposed, direct or indirect, near-term or far-term. Reassess as soon as a trigger appears: an announcement, a competitor launch, an enforcement date.

3.title: Assess and Triage an External Change
3.text: First confirm the facts: what exactly changed, who it applies to, and the effective date. Then assess the impact on objectives, the business case, scope and backlog. Assess schedule, cost and risk. And assess compliance and suppliers. Respond in proportion. A mandatory dated requirement: comply by the effective date. A threat to value: take it to the sponsor and governance to revalidate the business case. An uncertain or proposed change: monitor, assess the potential impact, define triggers, and do not cut scope on speculation. An opportunity: an active response. A dependency: coordinate and model it.

3.title: Prioritizing the Impact
3.text: Prioritize the impact on scope or backlog. Mandatory and dated items come first: they are not negotiable, and the effective date sets the latest start. Then weigh value and cost of delay, effort against lead time, the risk of doing nothing, dependencies including external approvals, and the opportunity window. Then act through the right channel. In adaptive work, the product owner reprioritizes the backlog and updates the roadmap. In predictive work, raise a change request. If value is threatened, go to the sponsor and governance.

3.title: Situations the Exam Likes
3.text: Some situations the exam likes. A known regulation takes effect in a year: assess the impact and reprioritize now. A competitor launches a cheaper product: reassess priorities and value, and take options to the sponsor. Sanctions hit a supplier's country, but deliveries are not yet affected: assess the supply impact and plan alternatives before deliveries stop. The market in the business case closes while the plan is on track: revalidate value with the sponsor. A trade agreement under negotiation: monitor, define triggers, and do not cut scope on speculation. A new technology that could halve processing time: plan an opportunity response.

3.title: Case Check-In: An External Change
3.text: Back to our microgrid. The utility announces a new tariff rule that changes the value of stored energy. Confirm the facts and the effective date. Assess the impact on the benefits, the controller logic, the backlog and contracts. Use the right channel: the product owner reprioritizes the software backlog, and baseline impacts go to the change board. And because the rule may change the business case, take it to Elena Vasquez to revalidate the value. Cost and schedule can stay on track while the business case changes.

3.title: Continually Review the External Environment
3.text: Continually review the external environment. Keep a standing cadence, and re-assess when a trigger appears. Keep assumptions and constraints current: an assumption about a market or regulation that is no longer true is a trigger. Report honestly to the sponsor: what changed, the impact, options and a recommendation. A project may end early when the need no longer exists because of changes in strategy, priorities or the external environment. Reassessing value regularly is how you notice. And do not let good performance hide value erosion.

3.title: External Change in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
3.text: External change looks different by approach. Predictive: scan at initiation and planning, then at gates and status meetings. Absorb change through impact analysis, a change request and a baseline update. Mandatory items are added by controlled change, and the business case is revalidated at gates. Agile: scan at refinement, planning, reviews and retrospectives. The product owner reprioritizes the backlog and roadmap, with mandatory items at the top by effective date. Hybrid: formal control for the envelope, with the backlog inside.

3.title: Organizational and External Change Traps: What PMI Expects
3.text: The traps for organizational and external change. Evaluate the impact of organizational change with the sponsor first: do not pause everything, carry on unchanged, or decide alone. Brief a new sponsor. Plan the transition for reassigned staff. Assess culture before choosing the approach, and coach and tailor if there is a mismatch. For resistance, understand the cause and involve people. A known external change should reshape priorities now, and a changed market means revalidating the business case. Use the right channel, and scan routinely.

3.title: Module Recap
3.text: Let us recap the whole module. Change control: assess, decide at the right level, implement and update everything. Improvement: use lessons early, commit to a few tracked actions, and let asset owners update assets. Organizational change: evaluate with the sponsor, assess culture, and involve people. External change: scan routinely, triage, use the right channel, and revalidate value. Remember the four kinds of change: to the project, to the way of working, to the organization, and outside. Now it is time to test yourself. Five questions follow. For each one, pause the video, choose your answer, and then listen to the explanation.

3.title: Practice Question 1
3.text: Question one. A team lead tells the project manager that a free design improvement was already built into the product and has passed all tests. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. Even free or tested improvements are changes, so the project manager assesses the impact and submits it through change control, retroactively if it was already made. Keeping it, removing it automatically, or informal approval all skip the assessment and the record.

3.title: Practice Question 2
3.text: Question two. After every sprint retrospective, the team lists many good ideas, but nothing seems to change. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. Retrospective actions must be implemented: a few are committed, put in the next backlog with owners and checked, and the improvement process itself is adapted. More meetings, stopping them, or only logging ideas do not change anything.

3.title: Practice Question 3
3.text: Question three. A merger will change the platforms and vendors that the project depends on. What should the project manager do first? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. Organizational change is evaluated with the sponsor first, and then the actions are determined, with change control for baseline changes. Pausing everything, carrying on blindly, or deciding alone each skip the evaluation.

3.title: Practice Question 4
3.text: Question four. Staff say the new approval tool is a surveillance burden and keep using their old spreadsheets. What is the best response? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. Resistance rooted in a lack of visible benefit is addressed by connecting the purpose to outcomes people value and involving them in tuning the solution. Mandates, feature-only training, or escalation to force compliance harden resistance.

3.title: Practice Question 5
3.text: Question five. A new regulation will take effect in twelve months, and the team is midway through designing a feature that will not comply. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. A known mandatory change reshapes priorities now, so the impact is assessed and the mandatory work is prioritized ahead of its effective date. Finishing first, waiting, or an exemption request avoid planning for compliance.

3.title: Answers at a Glance
3.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: C. An already-made free change is assessed and submitted retroactively. Question two: A. Commit to a few tracked actions, not a longer list. Question three: D. Evaluate organizational change with the sponsor, then act. Question four: B. Connect the purpose to outcomes people value and involve them. Question five: C. A known mandatory change reshapes priorities now. That completes Module 12. Next, Module 13 covers the calculations the exam uses, with worked examples. See you there.
